claim: Bid is the price a buyer is willing to pay; ask is the price a seller is willing to accept; spread is their difference (sec. 1 para 1; glossary 'Bid–ask spread').

note: Page heading/title reads 'Understanding Disclosure Documents' (byline 27 Aug 2026) but the body is FINRA's 'Understanding Market Liquidity and Your Investments', canonical at https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/market-liquidity-risk (retrieved 200, datetime 2026-08-04, same sentences). Source record title misidentifies the document.

claim: FINRA links limited liquidity with greater difficulty transacting and wider spreads (sec. 1 para 1).
locator: Introduction paragraphs 1-2 ('finding a buyer ... might be difficult'; 'illiquid investments often have a wide bid-ask spread'); Why Market Liquidity Matters ('Large bid-ask spreads can reduce returns').

claim: Evidence limits: a narrow spread alone is not a complete liquidity measure; quantity/participants matter.
locator: Introduction paragraph 2-3: 'A narrow spread can indicate good liquidity but doesn't provide a complete picture on its own'; 'how many participants are trading at various prices'.

claim: The SEC notes that last-traded price need not equal the price obtained by a market order (sec. 1 para 2).
locator: Types of Orders, market order paragraph: 'the last-traded price is not necessarily the price at which a market order will be executed'.
note: Same paragraph: a market order 'generally will execute at or near the current ... ask (for a buy order)' and guarantees execution but not price; supports the chapter's 'buyer seeking immediate execution consumes an available ask'.

locator: Trade Execution Isn't Instantaneous, para 2: 'Because price quotes are only for a specific number of shares, investors may not always receive the price they saw on their screen'.

claim: Indications are not a guarantee of the final auction price.
